newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus opposition chief arrested as protest looms.
newsitem.headline: Belarus opposition chief arrested as protest looms.

text.p: Belarus police have arrested a prominent opponent of hardline President Alexander Lukashenko in what opposition officials on Friday described as an attempt to scare people away from a big street protest which might turn violent.

A leading member of the nationalist Popular Front -- which opposes Lukashenko's policy of forming some kind of union with neighbouring Russia -- was arrested for "interfering with the work of the police," a spokesman for the Front said.

The Front's nationalist passions were bound to be stirred still further by a report from Russia's Interfax news agency on Friday quoting President Boris Yeltsin as saying that plans for closer ties with Minsk could one day lead to a full merger.

Many of the 10 million Belarussians, including some of Lukashenko's opponents, support the idea of closer ties with Russia but fewer want complete union and Lukashenko has stressed the need for Belarus to keep its sovereignty.

Police raided the Front's headquarters overnight and detained Professor Yuri Khodyko, 53, who spent 20 days in prison last year for helping organise other anti-Lukashenko rallies which have become a regular event in the capital.
Opposition officials said one person was injured as activists tried to resist. The press office for the city police said it had received no information on the arrest.

Leaflets advertising anti-Lukashenko protests planned for later on Friday and Constitution Day on Saturday were confiscated in a similar raid on the headquarters of the Civic Union party two days ago, the party's leader said.

Minsk's mayor has appeared on state-controlled television in recent days warning people not to take part in the protests which have been partly banned -- protesters are allowed to take part in rallies but not to proceed through the town.

"The protest will go ahead anyway despite the authorities' attempts to scare the opposition," Stanislav Bogdankevich, leader of the Civic Union party, former central bank chief and head of the disbanded parliament's liberal bloc, said.
"The right to hold meetings, actions and demonstrations is guaranteed even in Lukashenko's puppet constitution," he added.
Such actions have turned violent in the past, like on March 10 when thousands turned out to vent their anger at the arrival of a group of Russian deputies to discuss integration.
Opposition officials said about 100 people were detained and at least two protesters were beaten in scuffles with police including another Front leader, Lyavon Barshchevski.

No reaction was available from the president's office but the press secretary for his policy-making Security Council, Vasily Baranov, accused the opposition of looking for a fight and of getting "more and more out of control".
Western institutions have heaped criticism on Lukashenko, especially for a referendum in November when he used a landslide win to rewrite the constitution and obtain sweeping powers.
The new constitution allowed him to restart his five-year term, extending it without elections by 2-1/2 years, restructure parliament and appoint half the constitutional court.
A loose union of nationalists, intellectuals and students mostly concentrated in Minsk opposes Lukashenko, a former farm boss who came to power on promises of union with Russia in 1994.
